interest: This file provides valuable insight into the extreme vulnerability of Japan's financial markets to both international monetary shocks and imperial foreign policy crises in the early 1930s. It captures the immediate market panic following Great Britain's abandonment of the gold standard in September 1931—intensified by the Mukden Incident in Manchuria—which threatened brokers with insolvency until the Nomura Bank intervened. Additionally, the file documents the domestic economic fallout from Japan's withdrawal from the League of Nations in 1933, the inflationary pressures following the reimposition of the gold embargo, and early government initiatives to consolidate strategic heavy industries through a state-controlled iron and steel merger. Finally, the memorandum on Dr. Worden illustrates the legal and diplomatic friction surrounding Western perpetual leaseholds in former treaty ports as Japan asserted fiscal sovereignty.
overview: This file (decimal file 894.5171, covering October 1931 to March 1933) contains U.S. State Department records, cross-reference sheets, and an internal memorandum concerning financial conditions, securities markets, and related legal issues in Japan. The file documents two major episodes of distress on the Tokyo Stock Exchange: the trading suspension in late September 1931 triggered by Britain's departure from the gold standard and heightened tensions in Manchuria and China, which was stabilized by an emergency loan from the Nomura Bank of Osaka; and the severe market collapse in February 1933, precipitated by post-gold embargo inflation, rising industrial costs, and Japan's announced secession from the League of Nations. In addition, the file includes a Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum addressing a tax exemption claim on perpetual lease property in Yokohama asserted by an American citizen, Dr. Worden, which the U.S. Embassy declined to support under existing treaties.

subfiles.about: Report on the suspension of trading on the Tokyo Stock Exchange in September 1931 following Britain's suspension of gold payments and the Manchurian crisis.
subfiles.summary: A State Department Document File Note (cross-reference sheet) for Despatch No. 351 from Edwin L. Neville in Tokyo, dated October 9, 1931, accompanied by an attached extract from the despatch. The report details the temporary closure of the Tokyo Stock Exchange from September 25 to September 28, 1931, after an overwhelming wave of selling orders threatened brokers with bankruptcy. The market break was triggered by Great Britain's suspension of gold payments in London and exacerbated by political anxiety over events in Manchuria and China. The immediate crisis was resolved through an emergency loan of 3,400,000 yen extended by the Nomura Bank of Osaka to exchange brokers as a joint obligation.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet with Attached Extract from Despatch No. 351 on Tokyo Stock Exchange Suspension

subfiles.about: Report on the collapse of the Tokyo stock market in February 1933, price indices, unfavorable trade balances, and an impending iron industry merger.
subfiles.summary: A State Department Document File Note for Despatch No. 1939 from Ambassador Joseph C. Grew, dated March 6, 1933, transmitting Section VI on General Economic and Financial Conditions. It details the February 1933 collapse of the Tokyo stock market, which wiped out approximately half a billion yen in security values due to currency inflation following the gold embargo, Japan's announced withdrawal from the League of Nations, and rising manufacturing costs. The extract also reports a 2.9 percent drop in Tokyo wholesale prices, an accrued unfavorable trade balance of 126,647,000 yen through March 1, and plans for a government-controlled merger of state-owned and private iron and steel enterprises.
subfiles.title: Cross-Reference Sheet with Attached Extract from Despatch No. 1939 on the Tokyo Stock Market Collapse and Economic Conditions

subfiles.about: Memorandum reviewing an American citizen's claim of income tax exemption on perpetual lease rental property in Yokohama.
subfiles.summary: A Department of State Division of Far Eastern Affairs memorandum evaluating Tokyo Embassy despatch No. 274 regarding Dr. Worden of Yokohama, who claimed exemption from Japanese income tax on earnings derived from perpetual lease property rentals. The memorandum concurs with the Embassy's finding that tax exemption on perpetual leases is not guaranteed by explicit treaty rights, regarding each lease as a private contract between the lessee and Japanese authorities. It concludes that the U.S. government cannot intervene diplomatically unless evidence demonstrates that Dr. Worden is subject to anti-American discrimination.
subfiles.title: Memorandum on Dr. Worden's Income Tax Exemption Claim on Perpetual Lease Property
